page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Gay-Lussac's law
lines: Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes: when
gases react, the volumes of the reacting gases
and of the gaseous products are in a simple
whole-number ratio, at the same temperature
steps.why: This law is the volume counterpart of the mass laws, and it holds only when every volume is measured at one temperature and pressure — that condition is part of the statement.
common_mistakes: Leaving out 'at the same temperature and pressure'.
Applying the law to solids or liquids. It is a law about gases only.
steps.memory_tip: Combining VOLUMES, gases only, same T and P — three conditions in one sentence.
steps.margin_note: The volume ratio in the example (1 : 1 : 2) makes the statement concrete.

steps.label: Avogadro's law

lines.text: Avogadro's law: equal volumes of all gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of molecules

lines: This is why the mole ratio of gases equals
steps.why: Avogadro's law explains Gay-Lussac's observation: if equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules, then whole-number molecule ratios appear as whole-number volume ratios.
common_mistakes: Writing equal MASSES instead of equal VOLUMES.
steps.memory_tip: Equal volumes, equal molecules — with T and P held the same.
steps.margin_note: The closing line linking mole ratio to volume ratio shows the two laws connect.
